# Volume 3 — Chapter XXVIII A June Evening

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“I wonder what it would be like to live in a world where it was always June,” said Nell, stepping through the dusk-filled orchard's blossoms and fragrance toward the steps of the front door, upon which Thirza and Mrs. Agatha sat discussing the funeral of Mrs. Samson Coates, an event they had gone to earlier that day. Between the two of them sat Lucy, attentively working on her schoolwork; Robin, however, sat cross-legged on the lawn, appearing as somber and downcast as his one dimple permitted.
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0000 }

“It would grow tiresome to you,” Thirza remarked, letting out a sigh.
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0001 }

“I suppose so; however, right at this moment I believe I would need a very long while to grow weary of it, provided it remained entirely as delightful as it is today. June is loved by everything. Robin-boy, what is the reason for this somber November expression during the season of blossoms?”
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0002 }

“I am simply weary and fed up with life,” declared the young cynic.
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0003 }

“By the age of ten? My goodness, that is so tragic!”
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0004 }

“I am not teasing,” declared Robin gravely. “I am dis—dis—disheartened”—producing the lengthy term with a heroic attempt.
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0005 }

“For what reason and to what end?” inquired Nell, taking a seat at his side.
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0006 }

“’sence the substitute instructor who arrived after Mr. Holmes fell ill assigned me ten arithmetic problems to complete by Monday. Working on them will consume my entire day tomorrow. Being forced to labor on Saturdays is unjust. Milty Gammon declared that he would refuse to do them, yet Thirza insists that I must. I really do not care for Miss Carson.”
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0007 }

“Do not speak of your instructor in that manner, Robin Farrow,” Mrs. Agatha remarked sternly. “Miss Carson is an exceptionally good young woman. She has no silliness in her.”
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0008 }

“That sounds far from appealing,” Nell chuckled. “I prefer folks to possess a touch of foolishness. However, I am disposed to think more highly of Miss Carson than you do. My eyes fell on her during last night's prayer-meeting, and her eyes are incapable of looking practical all the time. So, Robin-boy, be of good courage. ‘Tomorrow will bring another day’ and I will assist you with the arithmetic to the best of my ability. Do not squander this beautiful time between dusk and night fretting about sums.”
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0009 }

“Well, I won’t,” said Robin, cheering up. “If you assist me with the sums I’ll get ’em finished soon enough to go fishing with Milty. I wish old Aunt Drusilla’s funeral took place tomorrow rather than today. I wanted to attend it ’cause Milty mentioned his mother said Aunt Drusilla would certainly sit up in her coffin and speak sarcastic things to the people who come to watch her buried. But Thirza claimed she wouldn’t.”
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0010 }

“In her casket, poor Drusilla was lying quite peacefully,” Mrs. Sowerby remarked with gravity. “That is the truth, I had not seen her appear so agreeable previously. Ah, over that poor old woman, not many tears were wept. To be free of her brings gratitude to the Elisha Ducketts, and I am unable to say that I fault them in the least.”
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0011 }

“It appears to me an utterly terrible prospect to depart from this life and leave not a single soul behind who grieves your passing,” Nell stated, trembling.
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0012 }

“No one besides her mother and father ever cared for poor Drusilla, indeed, not even the man she married,” declared Mrs. Sowerby. “She became his fourth spouse. Marrying had turned into a bit of a routine for him. His life ended just a couple of years following their wedding. Indigestion was the cause of death according to the doctor, yet I will constantly insist his passing was brought on by Drusilla’s mouth, precisely that. Poor thing, she was perpetually informed concerning all the details of her neighbors, although she remained quite unfamiliar with her own self. Ah well, she has passed away regardless; and I imagine Isolde’s marriage will be the upcoming commotion.”
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0013 }

“Thinking about Isolde getting married appears strange and dreadful,” Nell murmured, clasping her knees as her gaze went through the opening in the Whispering Wood toward the glow radiating from Isolde’s bedroom.
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0014 }

“She is prospering so much that the situation does not seem terrible to me,” Mrs. Sowerby declared with emphasis. “The farm owned by Gideon Duckett is excellent, and his character as a youth is exemplary.”
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0015 }

“Isolde may have once desired a husband who was wicked, dashing, and wild, but he is surely not that,” Nell said with a smile. “Gideon possesses immense goodness.”
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0016 }

“Precisely what he should be, that is. Is a wicked husband what you would desire for Isolde? Or for your own self?”
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0017 }

“Oh, no. Marrying a person who was evil is not something I would want, yet I believe I would enjoy it if he possessed the ability to be evil but chose not to be. As for Gideon, his goodness is beyond all hope.”
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0018 }

“I hope that one day you will possess greater wisdom,” Thirza expressed.
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0019 }

There was a certain bitterness in Thirza’s tone. Her disappointment was severe. She was aware that Nell had declined Hugh Carrow’s proposal. The rumors in Brierley hummed with this news, which had escaped, though no one could say how. It was possible that Wilfred Mott had surmised the truth and reported his assumptions as facts. Or perhaps Isolde had disclosed the matter to Gideon, who then acted without discretion. Whatever the case, the secret was out; Mrs. Carrow ceased asking Nell, whether in company or in confidence, if she had received recent news from Hugh, choosing instead to ignore her with a cold nod. Nell, who had ever held a fond affection for Hugh’s cheerful, youthful-spirited mother, felt a quiet sorrow because of this demeanor. Thirza kept silent; however, Mrs. Sowerby subjected Nell to numerous sharp, annoyed remarks on the subject, continuing until new rumors arrived to that respectable woman, via the mother of Elias Purdy MacKinnon, claiming that Nell had a different “beau” at university, one who combined wealth, attractive looks, and virtue. Following those reports, Mrs. Agatha kept quiet, even if her deepest desire remained that Nell had agreed to marry Hugh. Wealth was certainly desirable; yet even Mrs. Agatha, despite her pragmatic nature, did not view it as the sole necessity. Should Nell “like” this Handsome Unknown more than she did Hugh, there was no further room for argument; nevertheless, Mrs. Agatha was terribly anxious that Nell might commit the error of taking a husband for financial gain. Thirza understood Nell far too thoroughly to harbor such a worry; yet she suffered a conviction that something within the grand order of the universe had suffered a dismal disruption.
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0020 }

“Whatever is destined to occur will occur,” Mrs. Agatha remarked dejectedly, “and occasionally things that aren't meant to be come to pass anyway. Unless Providence steps in, I cannot refrain from thinking that this will take place regarding Nell, I really do.” Mrs. Agatha uttered a sigh. It was her fear that Providence would fail to step in; and she lacked the courage to do so herself.
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0021 }

Nell had drifted down toward the Nymph’s Well, curling herself up amid the ferns by the base of the large white birch where Hugh and she had spent so many moments together during past summers. Once college ended, he had returned to the newspaper office, making Brierley feel exceedingly dull in his absence. Since he never sent her any mail, Nell pined for those letters that failed to arrive. Naturally, Cyril wrote two times each week; his letters were delicate works of art that would have made wonderful reading inside a memoir or biography. Reading them made Nell feel that she was even more profoundly in love with him than before; nevertheless, her heart did not experience that strange, rapid, aching leap upon seeing his letters that it had felt on the occasion when Mrs. Hiram Mott passed her an envelope bearing Hugh’s dark, vertical penmanship. Nell had rushed back to the east gable and unsealed it with great anticipation—merely to discover a typewritten duplicate of a college society report—“only that and nothing more.” Nell threw the innocent document to the far side of her room and seated herself to compose a particularly sweet message to Cyril.
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0022 }

Five days remained until Isolde’s wedding. The gray dwelling located at Pear Hill was chaotic with baking, brewing, boiling, and stewing, because a grand, old-fashioned wedding was going to take place. Nell, naturally, was going to serve as bridesmaid, fulfilling a pact they had made at twelve years of age, and Hugh was traveling from Portmaris to act as best man. Nell took pleasure in the commotion surrounding the different preparations, yet beneath everything she felt a quiet ache in her heart. In a way, her cherished longtime friend was being lost to her; Isolde’s future dwelling would be located two miles away from Grey Shutters, making their former unceasing closeness impossible to retain. Nell raised her gaze toward Isolde’s light, reflecting on how it had shone like a beacon for her over numerous years; however, it would shortly cease to gleam through the summer twilights. A pair of large, aching tears rose in her gray eyes.
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0023 }

“Oh,” it occurred to her, “how awful it is that individuals must mature—and wed—and transform!”
{: #nw-v03-c28-p0024 }
